DLP: What Every New Homeowner Must Know Before It Expires

The Defect Liability Period is the only window where the developer must fix defects for free. Here is how to use it properly.

28 Jul 20267 min readGO XPERT SOLUTION

When you collect the keys to a new home, a clock starts running. During the Defect Liability Period (DLP), your developer is contractually obliged to rectify defects in your unit at no cost to you. Once that period lapses, every repair becomes your expense — permanently.

Most owners lose this entitlement not because the developer refused, but because they did not identify the defects in time, or could not describe them well enough to be actioned.

Check your S&P first

The exact length of your DLP is stated in your Sale and Purchase Agreement. Do not rely on what a neighbour or a Facebook group tells you — read your own agreement and note the expiry date somewhere you will not forget it.

Do not wait until the last month

This is the most common and most expensive mistake. A proper defect list often triggers several rounds: you submit, the developer rectifies, you verify, and some items come back incomplete. Each round takes weeks.

If you only start one month before expiry, there is no time for that cycle. Start as early as possible after handover.

Rule of thumb: inspect within the first month of receiving your keys, and re-inspect after the developer's rectification work — well before the DLP ends.

A vague complaint is easy to dismiss

"The bathroom is leaking" can be argued with. A recorded moisture reading, a photograph, an exact location and a defect category cannot be brushed aside as easily.

This is the difference between a complaint and a defect report — and it is usually the difference between a repair happening and a repair being delayed until your DLP quietly expires.

Keep everything, dated

  • Your S&P agreement and handover documents
  • Every defect list you submitted, with the date it was submitted
  • All correspondence with the developer — emails, letters, messages
  • Every inspection and re-inspection report

If the matter ever escalates, this chronology matters as much as the defects themselves. It shows you acted within the period and that the developer did not respond adequately.

Verify before you sign anything off

When the developer says the work is done, do not sign until it is verified. Cosmetic patch-ups are common: paint over a damp patch, silicone around a leaking joint, filler in a crack. Once you sign off, that item is closed and the entitlement is gone.
